name: Florence
info: Florence is a city on the Arno in Tuscany, Italy, founded by the Romans in 59 BCE as a colony for army veterans, later a trading and banking commune, the seat of the Medici and a birthplace of the Italian Renaissance.

facts.founded: Established by the Romans in 59 BCE as a colony for veteran soldiers, in an area previously inhabited by an Etruscan settlement whose name is unknown.
facts.where: In a basin ringed by hills on the Arno river in Tuscany, in central Italy, about 275 kilometres north-west of Rome.
facts.known: The gold florin; merchant banking; the Medici; the Italian Renaissance; Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio; Brunelleschi's dome; Savonarola; the first opera; capital of the Kingdom of Italy from 1865 to 1871
facts.today: Florence is the capital of the Italian region of Tuscany and of its metropolitan province, with a population of 361,625.

t: Florence began as a Roman colony of 59 BCE, became a self-governing commune in 1115, and grew rich on textiles, banking and the gold florin, first struck in 1252.
The Medici, bankers to the pope, governed the city from 1434 except for two periods of republican rule, and became hereditary dukes and then Grand Dukes of Tuscany in 1569.
Its artists, architects and writers made it a birthplace of the Italian Renaissance, and the Florentine dialect of Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio became the base of standard Italian.
dyk: The dome of Santa Maria del Fiore was proposed by Brunelleschi when the Florentines had begun building the cathedral without any design for a dome, and it remains the largest brick dome of its kind in the world.
ev: The Romans establish Florentia as a colony for veteran soldiers
Florence becomes the capital of the Tuscia region
The city is governed by an autonomous commune
The Medici take power, ending the Albizzi's sway
Savonarola is hanged and burned in the Piazza della Signoria
Cosimo I is made Grand Duke of Tuscany
Florence replaces Turin as capital of the Kingdom of Italy

sections.origins:
Florence lies in a basin ringed by hills, on the Arno, with three smaller rivers, the Mugnone, Ema and Greve, and some streams flowing through it. For much of the Quaternary the plain of Florence, Prato and Pistoia held a great lake, and ponds and marshes remained until the land was reclaimed in the 18th century. It is thought that a settlement stood at the confluence of the Mugnone and the Arno between the 10th and 8th centuries BCE. Between the 7th and 6th centuries BCE the Etruscans found and used a ford of the Arno near that confluence, and a bridge or ferry was probably built about ten metres from the present Ponte Vecchio. They preferred not to build on the plain, for reasons of defence, and settled on a hill about six kilometres away, at the fortified centre of Vipsul, today's Fiesole.

Written history traditionally begins in 59 BCE, when the Romans founded a village for army veterans, built in the style of an army camp. According to some stories Caesar wanted an outpost near Fiesole to watch the roads and communications. Some historians argue that a pre-Roman settlement existed, possibly destroyed by Sulla. The town was first named Fluentia, because it stood between two rivers, and the name later changed to Florentia, meaning the Flourishing Town. It lay on the Via Cassia, the main route between Rome and the north, and the Romans built ports on the Arno and the Mugnone.
sections.growth:
The Roman settlement quickly became an important commercial centre. Around the military camp the Romans built an aqueduct from Monte Morello, a forum in what is now the Piazza della Repubblica, baths, a theatre and an amphitheatre, and in 123 CE a bridge over the Arno. They organised the surrounding land by centuriation, and a nearby river port allowed trade up to Pisa.

After the early Middle Ages Florence revived. In 1100 it was a commune, and its primary resource was the Arno, which gave power for industry, mainly textiles, and access to the sea for trade. Florentine merchant bankers brought financial innovations such as bills of exchange and double-entry bookkeeping to medieval fairs. The gold florin, introduced in 1252, was the first European gold coin struck in sufficient quantities to play a significant commercial role since the 7th century, and it became the dominant trade coin of Western Europe. Florentine banks had branches across Europe, and Florentine bankers financed the English kings during the Hundred Years' War and the papacy. The city had 50,000 people in 1200, and by 1300 its population was 120,000, with a further 300,000 in the Contado. The 15th century, when its population was 60,000, was the age of the Medici and of the artists they patronised, among them Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci and Botticelli.
sections.rulers:
Florence was part of the Roman Republic and Empire, and in 285 CE it became the capital of Tuscia. It was then held by Odoacer, by the Ostrogoths, who alternated with the Byzantines in a struggle for the city, and from the 6th century by the Lombards. Charlemagne conquered it in 774, and it became part of the March of Tuscany, centred on Lucca. Margrave Hugh chose Florence as his residence instead of Lucca around 1000. In 1115 the city came under an autonomous commune, the Republic of Florence.

After the Albizzi family held sway from 1382 to 1434, the Medici took power. Cosimo de' Medici controlled the city from behind the scenes, and was followed by his son Piero and, in 1469, his grandson Lorenzo. Piero II was expelled in 1494 and a republic was restored. The Medici returned in 1512 with Spanish and papal troops, were driven out again in 1527, and came back in 1530 with the armies of Charles V. Alessandro de' Medici became the first Duke of Florence, and Cosimo I was named Grand Duke of Tuscany in 1569. The Medici reigned until Gian Gastone died in 1737.

Francis Stephen of Lorraine then took the throne, and Tuscany passed to the Habsburg-Lorraine dynasty. From 1801 to 1807 Florence was the capital of the Kingdom of Etruria, and from 1808 to 1814 the prefecture of the French département of Arno. The Habsburg-Lorraine rulers returned and were deposed in 1859, and Tuscany joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1861. Florence was its capital from 1865 to 1871.
sections.life:
Florence was long a city of guilds. After an anti-aristocratic movement led by Giano della Bella, the Ordinances of Justice of 1293 shifted power from the aristocracy to the merchants and members of organised guilds. In the Renaissance city the highest executive authority, the Signoria, was formed by drawing names from bags, one for each sixth of the city, every two months, a lottery that organised the political structure until 1434. Mobs were both common and influential, and families struggled constantly for power.

About 25,000 people were engaged in the wool industry. In 1338 there were about 17,000 beggars in the city, 4,000 of them on public relief, and six primary schools taught 10,000 pupils, including girls. Four high schools taught 600 students. The richest 10% of the population owned 68% of the wealth and the poorest 60% just 5%. The University of Florence was first founded in 1321.

Eastern merchants, some from the Oltrarno quarter, brought the cult of Isis and later Christianity to Roman Florence, and the city was the seat of a bishopric from around the beginning of the 4th century. Most of its people later belonged to the Roman Catholic Church. In the 14th century the Florentine dialect, in the works of Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio, became the basis of a national literary language. A foreign community came to make up about one quarter of the population in the second half of the 19th century.
sections.crises:
In the early Middle Ages Ostrogoths and Byzantines fought over Florence, taking it by siege and losing it again, and by the 6th century the population had fallen to as few as 1,000, according to speculation. In the 13th century the city was divided by the struggle between the Ghibellines, supporters of the German emperor, and the pro-papal Guelphs, which began after the murder of the nobleman Buondelmonte del Buondelmonti. The Guelphs split into White and Black factions, and the White Guelphs were exiled, among them Dante, who was sent into exile in 1301. The Black Death reduced the population by over half, and in 1378 the wool workers rose in the Revolt of the Ciompi.

On 26 April 1478 Jacopo de' Pazzi and his retainers tried to raise the city against the Medici, murdering Giuliano di Piero de' Medici and wounding his brother Lorenzo. On 23 May 1498 Savonarola was hanged and burned on the Piazza della Signoria and his ashes were dispersed in the Arno. The ten-month siege of 1529 to 1530 ended the Republic and brought the destruction of the suburbs, the ruin of the export business and the confiscation of citizens' wealth.

In the Second World War Allied bombers struck central Florence on 25 September 1943, destroying many buildings and killing 215 civilians. In August 1944 the retreating Germans demolished the Arno's bridges except the Ponte Vecchio. Florence was liberated on 4 August 1944. On 4 November 1966 the Arno flooded the centre, killing at least 40 people and damaging millions of art treasures and rare books. A car bomb in 1993 killed five people behind the Uffizi.
sections.legacy:
Many academics consider Florence the birthplace of the Renaissance, and Florentine artists and architects such as Brunelleschi, Donatello, Masaccio, Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo worked there. The cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore was begun in 1296 to a design of Arnolfo di Cambio and structurally completed by 1436 with Brunelleschi's dome, which is still the largest brick dome of its kind in the world. Michelangelo's David was made between 1501 and 1504. The Uffizi was founded on a large bequest from the last member of the Medici family, and the church of San Lorenzo holds the Medici Chapels. Santa Croce is the burial place of Michelangelo, Galileo and Machiavelli.

Florence also left its language. The Florentine dialect became the base of standard Italian, through the works of Dante, Petrarch, Boccaccio, Machiavelli and Guicciardini. Opera was invented in Florence in the late 16th century, when Jacopo Peri's Dafne was first performed, and the piano was invented there in 1709 by Bartolomeo Cristofori. Two Medici were popes, Leo X and Clement VII, and Catherine and Marie de' Medici became queens of France.

The centre is contained in medieval walls built in the 14th century, and the outline of the Roman city is still recognisable in its plan. The historic centre was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1982. Florence is today the capital of Tuscany, with a population of 361,625.

summary: Florence, on the Arno in Tuscany, was founded by the Romans in 59 BCE and became a wealthy commune of merchants and bankers. Under the Medici it was a birthplace of the Renaissance, and it was the capital of the Kingdom of Italy from 1865 to 1871.
references: Gene A. Brucker, The Society of Renaissance Florence: A Documentary Study (New York, Harper & Row, 1971)
R. W. B. Lewis, The City of Florence: Historical Vistas and Personal Sightings (Farrar, Straus, and Giroux, 1996)
Ferdinand Schevill, History of Florence: From the Founding of the City Through the Renaissance (New York, Harcourt, Brace and Co, 1936)
Christine Sciacca, Florence at the Dawn of the Renaissance: Painting and Illumination, 1300–1500 (Getty Publications, 2012)
notes: BLACK DEATH YEAR: the main article gives 1348; the History article gives 1349 (for the population estimate) and 1348 (Villani's death). I left the year out of the text and out of the events.

POPULATION c. 1300: the main article says the urban population 'may have been as great as 120,000' at the height around 1325, and its Demographics section gives 120,000 'by 1300' plus 300,000 in the Contado; I used the 1300 figure. The History article estimates 80,000 before the Black Death. Not reconciled; the 80,000 is left out.

ALESSANDRO: the main article says Florence became a monarchy in 1531 with Alessandro as Duke of the Florentine Republic; the History article says the title Duke of Florence was arranged in 1532 and that he ruled 1531 to 1537. I gave no year for the title.
MEDICI RETURN 1530 and the siege 1529-1530: the History article says the siege ended the Republic and Alessandro became ruler. Text follows both.
The Pazzi plot and Savonarola dates come from the main article's Piazza della Signoria list. Savonarola's excommunication is from the main article.

START is the Roman foundation of 59 BCE as both articles give it; the History article adds a possible earlier settlement (10th-8th centuries BCE; Etruscan ford 7th-6th), and some historians' pre-Roman town destroyed by Sulla, all hedged in the text.

In the History article's text the Roman Empire dates, and the 'Lombard 6th century' are as given; 'Odoacer' and 'Ostrogoths' come from the infobox list of the main article. The infobox gives Lombard 570-773; I wrote 'from the 6th century'.
In 123 CE a bridge: the article writes 'AD 123'.
Left out: the cinema, video games, cuisine, tourism, sport, economy, transport, twin towns, mayors and political parties (not history), and the Stendhal syndrome.
The 1993 bombing is attributed to the Mafia in the History article; I did not name a perpetrator.
